extracted.intended_audience: general Wikipedia readers; researchers or members of the public seeking background on U.S. conservative/religious organizations
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia entry summarizing the history, operations, campaigns, controversies, and external reactions to the American Family Association (AFA). Intended to provide an overview and sourced claims about the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFA Journal content categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: AFA Journal reviews prime-time television shows and categorizes them based on profanity, sex, violence, homosexuality, substance abuse, 'anti-Christian' content, or 'political correctness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each review includes short descriptions of episode content, lists the advertisers of the show, and invites readers to contact advertisers or networks to express concern. Used as the basis for public campaigns (e.g., boycotts or advertiser pressure). Example: the journal's categorization accompanies calls-to-action.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFA boycott triggers (reasons for organizing boycotts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AFA has organized boycotts against companies for perceived promotion of indecency, obscenity, pornography, support of pro-choice activism, depiction or support of LGBTQ rights (including same-sex partner benefits), violent/sexual content in entertainment, and Christmas-related controversies (e.g., failing to mention Christmas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article gives multiple historical examples (7‑Eleven over Playboy, PepsiCo over Madonna, Disney over domestic partnership benefits, Target over transgender restroom policy, etc.). Tactics include letter-writing campaigns, action alerts to subscribers, advertisements, and urging consumers to avoid companies; outcomes vary (some companies change practices, others do not). The AFA also sometimes ends boycotts after perceived concessions or leadership changes (e.g., Disney after Eisner's departure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) hate-group listing criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: SPLC listed the AFA as an anti-LGBTQ 'hate group' for the 'propagation of known falsehoods' and for using 'demonizing propaganda' against LGBTQ people; SPLC's listings are based on propagation of known falsehoods and demonizing propaganda, not merely on religious belief that homosexual activity is sinful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records SPLC's rationale and notes responses from AFA and allied organizations. It also notes SPLC's statement that mere opposition to same-sex marriage does not by itself justify a 'hate group' listing. Examples and quotations from SPLC and reactions from politicians and other groups are provided in the article as context for this evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: CyberPatrol 'intolerance' classification standard
rubrics_metrics.description: CyberPatrol blocked the AFA website by classifying it under 'intolerance', defined as 'pictures or text advocating prejudice or discrimination against any race, color, national origin, religion, disability or handicap, gender or sexual orientation...', citing AFA statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes specific AFA statements CyberPatrol cited (e.g., advocating outlawing public homosexuality, claims linking homosexuality to societal decay) and notes AFA's objection that the blocking infringed free speech. This illustrates how third-party content filters evaluate sites against intolerance/discrimination criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria used by third parties to judge AFA's rhetoric/practices (propagation of falsehoods/demonizing propaganda/intolerance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple external actors (watchdogs, media, civil‑rights groups) evaluate the AFA on whether it spreads demonstrably false claims about LGBTQ people, uses demonizing language/propaganda, or promotes intolerance and discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents examples used by critics: repeated false or unsubstantiated claims (e.g., assertions linking homosexuality to Nazism or pedophilia), inflammatory language from AFA figures (Bryan Fischer, Scott Lively), and altered media re‑posts (OneNewsNow changing 'gay' to 'homosexual' in AP articles). These concrete examples are cited by critics and watchdogs (SPLC, Teaching Tolerance, ACLU, etc.) when applying their evaluative standards.
